notes: Every number is quoted from (or arithmetically derived from, with the derivation stated) a source listed on that entry. null means no defensible published value exists; nothing is interpolated.

height_m / mass_kg: male/female only where a source gives sex-specific figures; most fossils cannot be sexed, so 'mean' (a published taxon mean) is the value to scale by when male/female are null. range = published specimen range or published species range, as cited in 'basis'.
cranial_cc: endocranial volume in cc (= ml). brain_rel = cranial_cc.mean / modern.cranial_cc.mean (1330); it can exceed 1 (Neanderthals, Harbin) and that is real, not an error.

proportions.arm_to_leg, skull.* 0–1 scores are ordinal encodings for the procedural model, not measurements. Each is set from the sourced anatomical description quoted in that entry's 'basis'. Anchors: modern = 0.5 for arm_to_leg; for skull scores 0 = absent/modern-minimal, 1 = most extreme among the taxa in this file (P. boisei for face_width and jaw_size, Kabwe for brow_ridge).

Alias lookup: match a people 'name' from data/earth-humans.json against species[].alias. If the species has alias_eras for that name, the era year must also match. Otherwise, any name in modern_aliases (or 'Homo sapiens' in the eras listed in modern_alias_eras) renders as a modern human. Names in unmapped_aliases have no figure.
confidence: high = multiple skeletons with body-size estimates; medium = partial skeletons or few specimens; low = body plan largely unknown.

height_m.basis: Global mean adult height for people born 1996: men 171 cm, women 159 cm (NCD-RisC 2016, as summarised by Our World in Data).

mass_kg.basis: mean: global average adult body mass 62 kg in 2005 (Walpole et al. 2012). male/female DERIVED: NCD-RisC 2016 global age-standardised mean BMI 2014 (men 24.2, women 24.4 kg/m²) × height² (1.71 m, 1.59 m) = 70.8 kg and 61.7 kg, rounded.

cranial_cc.basis: 89 cranially diverse present-day humans: mean 1328 ± 164 ml, range 1082–1832 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018), rounded to 1330. Smithsonian gives ~1300 cc; ~1350 cc is the commonly quoted round figure.

skull.basis: Smithsonian: thin-walled, high vaulted skull with a flat, near-vertical forehead; much less (if any) brow ridge and prognathism; smaller jaws and teeth than earlier humans.

modern_aliases_note: All peoples in eras from -5000 onward (cultures, states, empires, countries) are also anatomically modern; they are not listed individually. 'Sulawesi cave artists' are inferred to be H. sapiens from the art, not from fossils.

unmapped_aliases.Unknown toolmakers: Loess Plateau stone tools ~2.1 Ma; no fossils, maker's species unknown, so no figure.

species.name: Homo erectus

height_m.basis: mean: H. erectus sensu lato 163.4 cm, n=21 (Will et al. 2017, Table 4). range: 145–185 cm (Smithsonian). Smithsonian gives no sex split because most fossils cannot be sexed.

mass_kg.basis: mean: H. erectus s.l. 60.8 kg, n=24 (Will et al. 2017). range: 40–68 kg (Smithsonian). Grabowski et al. 2015 equations give lower means (Asian 51.4 kg; African+Georgian 50–51 kg, as reported by Garvin et al. 2017).

cranial_cc.basis: mean: H. erectus sample 919 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018). range low: Dmanisi Skull 5, 546 cc (Lordkipanidze et al. 2013); high: Ngandong 14, 1127 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018 Table 1). Australian Museum quotes an average of ~1050 cc.

proportions.basis: Smithsonian: early African fossils had 'relatively elongated legs and shorter arms compared to the size of the torso'. Turkana Boy is tall and linear; Australian Museum notes thicker limb bones and shorter, stockier Chinese bodies. Dmanisi adult humerofemoral index 76.4 (Jungers et al. 2016) is less leg-elongated.

skull.basis: Australian Museum: 'a massive brow ridge', 'a low, sloping forehead', a midline keel (not a crest), jaw 'large and thick without a pointed chin'.

species.known_from: Trinil 2, Turkana Boy (KNM-WT 15000), Dmanisi, Zhoukoudian, Sangiran, Ngandong
species.note: Body nearly our size and shape, but a brain about two-thirds ours under a heavy brow.

species.name: Homo habilis

height_m.basis: male/female: ~130 cm / ~110 cm (Australian Museum). range: 100–135 cm (Smithsonian). Will et al. 2017 give 147 cm (n=7) but include femora (KNM-ER 1472, 1481) that may belong to H. erectus or H. rudolfensis.

mass_kg.basis: mean: ~32 kg (Smithsonian); 32.6 kg with Grabowski et al. 2015 equations (as reported by Garvin et al. 2017). range: 27.3–38.4 kg, n=3 (Jungers et al. 2016). Will et al. 2017's 48.4 kg includes contested specimens.

cranial_cc.basis: mean: ~610 cc (Australian Museum). low: KNM-ER 1813 ~500 ml (Australian Museum); high: OH 7 reconstruction 729–824 ml (Spoor et al. 2015).

proportions.basis: Australian Museum: OH 62 has 'relatively long arms and short legs'; limb proportions 'relatively ape-like'. Smithsonian: 'retains some ape-like features, including long arms'. No thorax known well enough to set torso.

skull.basis: Smithsonian: slightly larger braincase than Australopithecus, 'moderately-prognathic face', strong jaws with thick enamel. Australian Museum: 'a small, arched brow ridge'.

species.known_from: OH 7 (type), OH 24, OH 62, KNM-ER 1813, OH 8 foot
species.note: Roughly chest-high to us, with long ape-like arms and under half our brain.

species.name: Paranthropus boisei

height_m.basis: male/female: 137 cm / 124 cm (Smithsonian). range: P. boisei stature estimates 116–161.3 cm, n=6 (Will et al. 2017).

mass_kg.basis: male/female: 49 kg / 34 kg (Smithsonian). range: 28.4–51.6 kg, n=11 (Will et al. 2017).

cranial_cc.basis: mean: ~520 cc for P. boisei/robustus (Australian Museum). KNM-ER 406 ~510 cc (Australian Museum); OH 5 530 cc (eFossils). Range shown is these two specimens only.

proportions.basis: Smithsonian: a male boisei was 18 lb heavier than a male Au. africanus of the same height; strong sexual dimorphism. Limb proportions are not given by the cited sources; arm_to_leg set australopith-like (above modern) as an assumption — low certainty.

skull.basis: Smithsonian: strong sagittal crest; flaring cheekbones giving 'a very wide, dish-shaped face'; cheek teeth ~4× modern size; thickest enamel of any hominin. Australian Museum: males had the crest; KNM-ER 732 (female) lacks a large crest.

species.note: A face wider than ours on a child-sized body, with a bony crest anchoring huge chewing muscles.

species.name: Australopithecus sediba

height_m.basis: ~1.2 m (Australian Museum). MH1, a juvenile male of 12–13, was at most 1.3 m (Smithsonian). No adult stature has been published.

mass_kg.basis: Au. sediba 27.17 kg, range 22.7–29.7, n=3 (Will et al. 2017). Jungers et al. 2016: 25.9 kg (22.7–29.1, n=2).

cranial_cc.basis: MH1 endocast ~420 cc (Carlson et al. 2011; Australian Museum). Single juvenile.

proportions.basis: Smithsonian/Australian Museum: small body with 'relatively long upper limbs'. Schmid et al. 2013: ape-like narrow upper thorax, more human-like lower thorax.

skull.basis: Australian Museum: 'minimal cresting', 'weakly arched supraorbital torus', small cranium, no flaring cheekbones. Smithsonian: relatively small premolars/molars, Homo-like face.

species.posture: bipedal + climbing (walked on outer edge of the foot)
species.known_from: Malapa MH1 (juvenile male) and MH2 (adult female) partial skeletons
species.note: Chimp-sized brain and long climbing arms, but a face and hands already leaning toward Homo.

species.name: Homo naledi

height_m.basis: mean: ~1.44 m (Smithsonian); 143.6 cm (Garvin et al. 2017). male: ~150 cm (Australian Museum; females 'slightly shorter'). range: humerus/tibia estimates 139–156 cm (Garvin et al. 2017).

mass_kg.basis: mean/range: 20 postcranial specimens, mean 44.2 kg, range 35.2–52.9 kg (Garvin et al. 2017); Grabowski-equation mean is lower, 37.4 kg. male: ~45 kg (Australian Museum). Smithsonian: 39.7–55.8 kg.

cranial_cc.basis: Dinaledi composite crania 465 cc and 560 cc (Garvin et al. 2017); Lesedi LES1 ~610 ml (Australian Museum). No published species mean.

proportions.basis: Garvin et al. 2017: humero-tibial index 79.4, within the modern human (Kulubnarti) interval; elongated lower limb. Australian Museum: ribcage 'relatively broad like that of A. afarensis', australopith-like shoulders, long slender legs.

skull.basis: Australian Museum: 'well-developed supraorbital torus … with a weak arch'; lacks the long, low vault of H. erectus; back of skull curved sharply. brain_rel null because no mean; 465–610 cc is 0.35–0.46 of modern.

species.known_from: Dinaledi Chamber (1,550+ specimens, ≥15 individuals) and Lesedi Chamber (LES1), Rising Star Cave
species.note: Lived alongside early Homo sapiens, yet its brain was only a third to under half of ours.

sources.title: Smithsonian Human Origins – Homo naledi

species.name: Homo heidelbergensis (Kabwe / Broken Hill)
species.taxonomy_note: Kabwe 1 was named Homo rhodesiensis (Woodward 1921) and is usually filed under H. heidelbergensis. Roksandic et al. (published Oct 2021, print 2022) proposed retiring both names for African fossils and placing Kabwe and Bodo in Homo bodoensis; the proposal remains contested.

height_m.basis: male/female: 175 cm / 157 cm species averages (Smithsonian). range: early Mid-Pleistocene Homo 149.9–184.2 cm, n=13 (Will et al. 2017 Table 3). No stature has been published for the Kabwe skull's owner.

mass_kg.basis: male/female: 62 kg / 51 kg (Smithsonian). range: early Mid-Pleistocene Homo 47.1–82.6 kg, n=19 (Will et al. 2017 Table 3).

cranial_cc.basis: Kabwe 1: 1249 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018), ~1280 cc (Australian Museum), ~1300 cc (Smithsonian). Species average ~1250 cc (Australian Museum). low: Steinheim 1110–1200 cc (Australian Museum).

proportions.basis: Smithsonian: 'short, wide bodies'. Australian Museum: lower legs relatively long; leg bones thick and strongly built.

skull.basis: Smithsonian (Kabwe 1): 'large brow ridges', face flatter and less prognathic than H. erectus, low braincase, occipital torus. Australian Museum: 'a wide face, thick arching brow ridges and a sloping forehead'. No mandible known for Kabwe 1.

species.known_from: Kabwe 1 (Broken Hill, Zambia, 1921); also Mauer mandible (type), Bodo, Petralona, Arago
species.note: A brain nearly our size behind enormous, thick brow ridges and a wide face.

species.name: Homo neanderthalensis

height_m.basis: male/female: 164 cm / 155 cm (Smithsonian); Australian Museum gives 168 / 156 cm. mean/range: 162.7 cm, 148.7–181.2 cm, n=38 (Will et al. 2017).

mass_kg.basis: male/female: 65 kg / 54 kg (Smithsonian). mean/range: 70.5 kg, 53.0–90.5 kg, n=30 (Will et al. 2017).

cranial_cc.basis: Neanderthal sample mean 1450 ml (SD 189); Gibraltar 1 1213 ml to Amud 1 1747 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018). Australian Museum: average ~1500 cc.

proportions.basis: Smithsonian: shorter and stockier, 'thick, short lower arm and leg bones'. Australian Museum: shin and forearm both shortened, pelvis wider side to side, large joints. Both limbs shortened distally, so arm:leg ratio left at modern.

skull.basis: Australian Museum: 'thick but rounded brow ridge' under a 'flat and receding forehead'; occipital bun; no projecting bony chin; mid-face projects forward. Smithsonian: large midface, angled cheekbones, large nose.

species.known_from: Feldhofer (Neanderthal 1), La Chapelle-aux-Saints, La Ferrassie, Shanidar, Amud, Kebara
species.note: Shorter and far heavier-built than us, yet with a brain slightly larger than ours.

Will, Pablos & Stock (2017) R Soc Open Sci 4:171339
Neubauer, Hublin & Gunz (2018) Science Advances

species.name: Denisovans
species.years: about 200,000 – 50,000 years ago at Denisova Cave; Harbin ≥146,000; Penghu leg bones ~45,000 (preprint)

height_m.basis: Unknown in peer-reviewed literature. Best proxy (NOT peer-reviewed): Kaifu et al. 2026 bioRxiv preprint on protein-identified Penghu 2 femur and Penghu 3 tibia, Taiwan — roughly 1.76–1.90 m. Hawks cautions small comparative samples and trawling bias.

mass_kg.basis: Unknown in peer-reviewed literature. Same preprint reports >80 kg (Penghu 2 ~82.5 kg; Penghu 3 ~91 kg).

cranial_cc.basis: PROXY: Harbin cranium ~1420 ml (Ji et al. 2021), assigned to Denisovans by Harbin mtDNA (Fu et al. 2025, Cell) and proteome (Fu et al. 2025, Science). One individual.

proportions.basis: No associated postcranial skeleton. The Penghu leg bones (preprint) suggest a large, robust lower limb but say nothing about proportions.

skull.basis: Head shape PROXY = Harbin cranium (Ji et al. 2021): massive brow ridge, wide face, large long braincase. Jaws: Xiahe (Chen et al. 2019) and Penghu 1 (Tsutaya et al. 2025) mandibles are robust, chinless, with large molars.

species.posture: presumed fully bipedal (no postcranial skeleton to confirm)
species.known_from: Denisova Cave finger, molars and genome; Xiahe mandible (Tibet); Penghu 1 mandible (Taiwan); Harbin cranium (China)
species.note: Known mostly from DNA; the Harbin skull suggests a huge-browed, wide-faced head holding a brain bigger than ours.

species.name: Homo floresiensis

height_m.basis: LB1 (adult female) 106 cm (Brown et al. 2004; Smithsonian; Jungers et al. 2016 give 1.05 m). Only one skeleton; no male known.

mass_kg.basis: LB1 27.5 kg (Jungers et al. 2016; Grabowski et al. 2015 as reported by Garvin et al. 2017). range: ~25 kg (Australian Museum) to 30 kg (Smithsonian).

cranial_cc.basis: LB1: 380 cc originally (Brown et al. 2004); 426 cc by micro-CT (Kubo et al. 2013).

proportions.basis: Jungers et al. 2016: LB1 humerofemoral index 86.8, 'far outside the range of modern humans', femur 'especially short'. Australian Museum: feet 70% of femur length (modern 55%), wide pelvis, hunched shoulders. Build: 27.5 kg at 1.06 m = BMI ~24.5 (derived).

skull.basis: Australian Museum: long, low braincase like H. erectus; receding forehead; flat face; no chin; brow ridges not continuous; narrow nose. Smithsonian: large teeth for body size.

species.known_from: LB1 near-complete female skeleton and up to 12 individuals, Liang Bua cave, Flores
species.note: About one metre tall, with a chimpanzee-sized brain and feet 70% as long as its thigh.

species.name: Homo luzonensis
species.years: at least ~130,000 years ago (2023 uranium-series re-dating; first published as minimum ages of 67,000 and 50,000)

height_m.basis: Unknown: no long bones from adults. NHM: small teeth and foot bones suggest a short species, 'some estimates' under 1.2 m. Best proxy: H. floresiensis (1.06 m), the other small island hominin — a comparison, not an estimate.

proportions.basis: Only hand/foot bones, teeth and a child's femur. Curved finger and toe bones are australopith-like and may indicate climbing (Détroit et al. 2019; NHM).

skull.basis: No skull or mandible. Teeth are small, with a mix of primitive and modern-looking traits.

species.posture: bipedal + climbing (inferred from curved finger and toe bones)
species.known_from: 13 fossils from ≥3 individuals, Callao Cave, Luzon: teeth, finger and toe bones, juvenile femur
species.note: Tiny teeth and curved, climbing-style finger and toe bones; nothing else of its body is known.

sources.title: Détroit et al. (2019) A new species of Homo from the Late Pleistocene of the Philippines. Nature 568:181–186

species.name: Early Homo sapiens (Jebel Irhoud)
species.years: about 315,000 ± 34,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud); our species to present

height_m.basis: PROXY: no stature published for Jebel Irhoud. Middle Palaeolithic H. sapiens (mostly ~120–90 ka: Skhul, Qafzeh etc.) 173.8 cm, range 158.5–191.4, n=13 (Will et al. 2017 Table 4).

mass_kg.basis: PROXY: Middle Palaeolithic H. sapiens 62.7 kg, range 42.7–76.9, n=11 (Will et al. 2017 Table 4).

cranial_cc.basis: Jebel Irhoud 1 1375 ml and Irhoud 2 1467 ml (Neubauer et al. 2018); mean derived. Omo 2 (~195 ka) 1491 ml.

proportions.basis: Jebel Irhoud is known mainly from skulls, jaws and teeth; body shape taken from the MP H. sapiens proxy (modern-like). Assumption.

skull.basis: Hublin et al. 2017: face shape 'almost indistinguishable' from living humans, but an elongated, archaic braincase (not globular) and very large teeth. Chin of the Irhoud 11 mandible not characterised in the cited sources.

species.known_from: Jebel Irhoud 1, 2, 10 crania and Irhoud 11 mandible (Morocco); Omo Kibish I (Ethiopia)
species.note: Our face and brain size, but a long, low braincase not yet rounded like ours.
